title: Hype or Real?
hook: AI coverage swings between 'this changes everything' and 'it's all a bubble.' The truth is usually in between — and a few questions help you judge any big AI claim for yourself.
key_points: Both boosters and doomers have incentives to exaggerate — follow the motive.
Watch for vague demos, cherry-picked examples, and 'coming soon' that never arrives.
Ask: what can it do *today*, reliably, for real people — not in a staged demo?
Real and overhyped at once: genuinely useful, routinely oversold.
content_html: Living through the AI moment means being shouted at from two directions. One camp insists every release "changes everything" and that your job, your industry, and life itself will be unrecognizable by next quarter. The other insists it's all smoke and mirrors — a bubble of overpriced autocomplete about to pop. Both make for great headlines, and both are usually overstated. Developing a little skepticism in each direction is one of the most useful AI-literacy skills there is, because the reality is almost always messier and more interesting than either slogan.
extra_html: Start by following the incentives. Companies and the people invested in them have every reason to overhype — it sells products, attracts users, and raises money — so a glossy launch is marketing, not evidence. But doom has its own market: dramatic warnings draw clicks, attention, and influence, and "this could end the world" is a powerful way to be taken seriously. Knowing who benefits from a claim helps you weight it. Then watch for the classic tells of hype: slick demos that may be staged or cherry-picked, impressive one-off examples that don't hold up in everyday use, and the perennial "coming soon" that quietly never ships (remember all those "fully self-driving next year" promises). The single best filter is to ask: what can this actually do today, reliably, for ordinary people — not in a controlled demo, but in real hands? Finally, hold a both/and view, because it's the honest one: today's AI is genuinely useful and routinely oversold at the same time. It's already changing real work and real lives, and much of what's promised is exaggerated, premature, or vaporware. Treating "is this hype or real?" as a question to investigate — rather than a side to pick — is exactly how you stay grounded while everyone else is busy being amazed or outraged.

related.title: What AI Can't Do
related.hook: Today's AI can write a sonnet and flunk a question a child gets right. Knowing its hard edges — no real understanding, no live truth, no common sense — is what makes you good at using it.

related.title: AGI & Superintelligence
related.hook: AGI means AI as broadly capable as a human; superintelligence means far beyond. Both are goals and hypotheses — not products you can buy — and experts deeply disagree on when, or if.

related.title: Who Controls AI?
related.hook: The most powerful AI models are built by a handful of giant companies, because training them costs a fortune. Who holds that power — and whether 'open' AI can balance it — shapes everything.

related.title: The Leading AI Company Is Losing Billions a Year
related.hook: Leaked, audited financials reportedly show OpenAI bleeding billions of dollars a year. Its revenue is growing fast — but the cost of building AI is growing faster.

flashcards.prompt: What's the best question to cut through AI hype?

choices.text: What can it actually do today, reliably, for real people?
How impressive is the launch demo?
How much money did the company raise?

flashcards.explanation_html: Demos and funding aren't capability. Ask what works reliably right now for ordinary users — that filters marketing from reality.

flashcards.prompt: Why do both AI 'boosters' and 'doomers' tend to exaggerate?
flashcards.back_html: Incentives: hype sells products and raises money; dramatic doom draws attention and influence. Follow the motive behind a big claim.
